quick.summary: Stop building the first solution you are handed by your stakeholders.
quick.takeaway: Treat every feature request as a symptom of an unknown disease.

parts.title: Frame the real problem

beats.line: Product wants me to add a giant map to the home screen.
But a map makes the screen too cluttered. What should I do?
Think of a patient walking into a medical clinic.
They demand an arm cast. Does the doctor just build it?
No. The doctor asks where it hurts and takes a scan.
Right. The cast is a proposed solution, not the actual disease.
In design, we call this premature convergence.
Can I just say jumping to a solution?
Absolutely. Your product manager handed you a cast, not a diagnosis.
So how do I find out what the disease is?

parts.cliff: You have to become the doctor.

beats.line: A map request is just an attempt to solve a hidden problem.
Ask what fails if they do not get the map.
They said users are getting lost in the city.
Getting lost is the problem. The map is just one guess.
We could just send a text with directions instead.
Exactly. Framing the problem as getting lost gives you options.
And a text message takes one day to build, not two months.
Now you are thinking like a principal designer.
So I ask what breaks without the feature to find the problem.
Treat every request as a symptom, and find the cure.

quiz.question: A stakeholder demands a specific popup window. What is your first step?
options: Ask what breaks if the popup is not built.
Design the popup exactly as they asked.
Tell them popups are bad user experience.
Build a faster version of the popup.
quiz.explanation: The popup is just a proposed solution. You must find the underlying disease first.

quiz.question: Jumping to a solution saves time when the stakeholder already knows what they want.
quiz.explanation: It often wastes time by building a solution for the wrong problem, like giving a cast for a headache.
